newsitem.title: USA: California blazes dampened by wind shift.
newsitem.headline: California blazes dampened by wind shift.

text.p: Fierce hot winds that fueled a rash of wildfires in tinder-dry southern California died down on Wednesday, allowing firefighters to gain the upper hand.
The federal government issued an emergency declaration for the California counties of Los Angeles, Orange and San Diego due to fire damage, a spokesman for Gov. Pete Wilson said.
This would make residents who have been displaced as a result of the fires eligible for temporary housing assistance, spokesman Ron Low said.
The federal declaration would also allow local agencies to recover fire response costs and overtime costs incurred fighting the blazes, Low said.

Weather forecasters said the Santa Ana winds, which had roared across the region at more than 50 mph (80 kph), fell to 15 mph (25 kph) and disappeared later in the day. Humidity rose as sea breezes took over.
But meteorologists said the Santa Ana winds could return again at the weekend, raising fears of renewed fires.

The wind-blown wildfires erupted on Monday from the movie star colony of Malibu to mountains along the Mexican border, destroying or damaging more than 100 homes, injuring 11 people and burning some 35,000 acres (14,000 hectares) of land.

Firefighters said the blaze in Malibu, which burned nearly 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares), was 33 percent contained. It was believed to have started when a power line came in contact with a eucalyptus tree.
The big blaze in Carlsbad, north of San Diego, was reported by firefighters to be 68 percent contained on Wednesday afternoon.
One fireman was fighting for his life after he and five colleagues were trapped in their fire truck on Tuesday when a wall of flames jumped a road in a canyon north of Los Angeles.
The man was listed in critical condition in the hospital with burns over 60 percent of his body and respiratory problems.
"Two rigs were out on the road and one of them stalled. They were engulfed and got burned, they couldn't get out," said Don Wittey of the Los Angeles Fire Department.
In the Santa Monica hills overlooking Malibu, some residents returned to their homes amid charred tree trunks and scorched brush.
Oliver Bendig was one of the unlucky ones, who found only smoldering ruins. "It was a beautiful home -- it's gone," he said, surveying the smoking debris. "It had windows, windows all around."
Another resident, Lloyd Smith, tried to salvage what he could from the ruins of his family house built 50 years ago.
"When I was growing up, I helped my dad build extensions," he said, adding that his $50,000 record collection had gone up in smoke.
The latest rash of wildfires struck almost three years to the day after a firestorm swept southern California, destroying nearly 1,000 homes and causing hundreds of millions of dollars in damage.

Jeff Harris lost his home in Malibu in 1993 and rebuilt in another canyon. The latest fire saw flames stop yards from his new house. "I couldn't believe it all happening again. It was so sad to see," he told local television.
Another resident, Jim Duffy, said the danger was constant: "It's scary. You never know which way the wind's going to turn."
